newsitem.title: HUNGARY: New Hungary privatisation chief sees big year ahead.
newsitem.headline: New Hungary privatisation chief sees big year ahead.

text.p: Judit Csiha, appointed Hungarian minister in charge of privatisation after scandal toppled her predecessor, says the far-reaching programme has, on balance, been a success despite some setbacks.

"It (the privatisation) was necessary. it supported the restructuring of the economy and it set Hungary on the path to a modern market economy," Csiha, appointed to run APV Rt in October, told Reuters in an interview. "It opened Hungary towards the world, it helped to balance the economy and it created the situation and changes setting the stage for the new integration (with Europe)," she added.

Csiha, named to the post after former industry and trade minister Tamas Suchman was sacked over irregular payments by APV amounting to millions of dollars (corrects from "tens of millions") to a consultant, said she did not think the scandal negated APV's usefulness.
Privatisations have brought more than 900 billion forints ($5.3 billion) to the government's coffers this decade.
Csiha said much of her work for the coming year would be to revamp the agency to run industries, including farm co-ops and forestry concerns, that will remain in state hands.

She also will oversee what promises to be the last big year of state-owned property selloffs, in which Hungary will dispose of shares in oil company MOL, national airline Malev, pharmaceuticals maker Richter and dozens of small or medium-sized companies which have proved hard to sell.
Csiha said selling the smaller companies was one of her primary goals.

"We tried to sell these companies but were not able to find buyers," she said in a wide-ranging interview on Friday. "These usually were companies that were in a difficult situation -- but there is the possibility that employee or management buyouts will be taken advantage of."

She said the government would improve the companies' marketability by boosting the ceiling for "simplified" privatisations to cover companies with subscribed capital of up to 800 million forints, up from the present 600 million cutoff.

"I've had discussions with companies in different countries and with different ambassadors and they say there is interest for smaller investment in Hungary," Csiha said. "So it is not true that everyone wants to spend more than $100 million."
For those with deep pockets, Hungary plans to sell a big tranche of MOL, the biggest-capitalised issue on the Budapest bourse.

Media reports have said APV would offer a 33 percent stake in MOL, part of it at the beginning of the year and part at the end, but with the government retaining a 25 percent plus one golden share, ensuring special voting rights.
With MOL shares soaring again on the Budapest bourse, after a rocky road last year when energy price increases were being debated, Csiha said the timing for the sale was opportune.
"MOL finished a very good year and it seems for the share issuing there is very significant interest," she said.

She said the government also hoped to obtain attractive offers for some remaining banks, among them Kereskedelmi and Hitel Bank, whose prospects soared with the $89.23 million sale of Magyar Hitel Bank to Dutch bank group ABN AMRO.

Csiha dismissed as "press rumours" reports that APV wants Italy's Alitalia to sell the 30 percent stake in Malev in bought in 1993, but she indicated Hungary would be casting around for other buyers when it sells part of its remaining 69.3 percent stake in the Hungarian carrier.

"What I can say about whether a sale is successful or not ...is that I think I can give you a correct answer only in the surroundings when it actually took place...and I don't think you can compare 1993 with the situation now," she said.
She said the best partner for Malev would be an airline that is growing and added, "We would welcome anyone who is interested, we would like to have our choice."
Csiha said she was not surprised by the debate that has swirled around Hungary's most ambitious privatisation to date, the sale of much of its energy sector to Western investors.
Some of the investors have claimed the government has set price increases too low to give them the eight percent return on investment from January 1997.
"I think the reason this got international publicity is because this is a very important business sector and the participants are important partners in the world and in Europe," she said.

She added that she did not think the Belgian utility group Tractebel, which has said it was considering taking legal action, would wind up selling back to the government its $141 million stake in the Dunamenti oil-fired power station station. ($ = 170.3 Hungarian Forints)
